In this regard, foreign cultural relations and education policy can make a significant contribution to bolstering civil society by linking actors with one another and enabling them to gain qualifications either in the country or in Germany.
Joint cultural projects show our Ukrainian partners that Europe has not forgotten them.
It would be naive to overestimate the effectiveness of cultural work in solving acute, warlike confrontations.
I am however firmly convinced that cultural exchange plays a key role in managing deeply-rooted societal conflicts.
What exactly do these projects, which bolster civil society and foster critical exchange, look like?
Here are a few examples of projects which the Goethe-Institut is running up to the end of this year:
Such programmes strengthen civil society discourse by providing journalists with qualifications and enabling them to build networks.
These journalists follow social change in their countries and thus the programmes help the public to develop the self-confidence to take positions on current affairs within their societies.

“Depeche Mode” is a theatre, music and literary project that seeks to bring people from different regions of Ukraine together for discussions.
It is based on the novel with the same name by the young Ukrainian author Serhiy Zhadan, which paints a moving and at the same time shockingly realistic picture of young people’s lives after the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Director Markus Bartl from Germany has adapted the novel to be performed on stage and in doing so, wants to initiate a discussion about social realities in today’s Ukraine.
Yet other crisis regions in the world also show how important stronger cultural engagement can be as part of a foreign policy aimed at building confidence.
As part of this, it is crucial that cultural institutes are able to offer a space of freedom.
For example, under Mubarak, films could be shown which would otherwise have been censored in Egypt.
The Tahrir Lounge serves as an example for many of the Goethe-Institut’s other meeting places in which people who live in crisis zones can discuss, work and organise themselves unhindered.
That is the case in the Middle East as much as it is in Ukraine.
It is thus ever more important to actively and sustainably support civil society groups who work in the fields of culture and education in these countries.
Precautionary foreign policy facilitates cultural encounters and networking before, during and after crises,
thus making it a key foundation of global understanding.

Liberia –
helping Ebola support staff
Handover of medical supplies to a health facility
The Ebola virus has been spreading in West Africa for months – above all in Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia.
The three countries are amongst the poorest in the world and are only just slowly recovering from years of political unrest.
With support from the Federal Foreign Office, the non-governmental organisation (NGO) Humedica is running a project on preventing and overcoming the disease in Liberia
– particular attention is being paid to the correct use of protective equipment in order to prevent medical support staff from being infected.
The aim is to reduce the number of medical support staff becoming infected with Ebola through improved prevention and control.
Due to a lack of protective equipment and knowledge of the risks of infection, more people are still becoming infected – this threatens to further reduce the already insufficient number of medical support staff.
Moreover, time and again a lack of knowledge about how to handle Ebola patients as well as insufficient disinfection material and protective equipment in health facilities have led medical support staff to flee or refuse to work for fear of becoming infected.
Correct use of protective equipment
The Humedica team in action
A particular focus of their work will be on training people in how to deal with suspected Ebola infections as well as how to put on, disinfect and dispose of protective equipment.
Furthermore, swiftly tracking cases of infection in rural areas and better coordinating the medical intervention should also help curb the epidemic.
Humedica distributing equipment which protects against Ebola
Humedica is thus making an important contribution to countering the epidemic.

A difficult balancing act
Aid organisations need to be independent.
This sounds simple and self-evident, but it is not.
Who provides humanitarian aid?
Respect and distance are needed!
Obviously, humanitarian organisations should and must resist this and insist on the primacy of helping all those in need to survive.
NATO, the EU and the German Government have drawn up comprehensive security and anti-terrorism strategies whose aims include the use of state-funded humanitarian aid as a strategic tool for political purposes.
Humanitarian aid needs countries’ support.
However, it also needs respect and distance, or better still, respect for distance!

Humanitarian aid is an important part of German foreign policy, but too often it runs the risk of being exploited for political purposes.
Humanitarian aid must not be an instrument of foreign and security policy
We call on the German Government to actively support humanitarian aid and to resolutely defend the autonomy of humanitarian aid against all political objectives that are contrary to its actual meaning and purpose.
By Florian Westphal and Ulrike von Pilar of Médecins Sans Frontières.
“The Federal Republic of Germany should play a leading role as regards supporting humanitarian aid in crisis-hit areas in North Africa, thus stemming the flows of refugees.”
(Mira Lüthe: “What values should Germany stand for worldwide?”)
One can see her point, and yet this type of statement makes us at Médecins Sans Frontières unhappy, as it shows a widespread misconception, namely that humanitarian aid is provided in order to stem the flows of refugees, create peace, consolidate security, stabilise countries, foster democracy, make development possible...
The list goes on and on!
These are all important goals, but they have nothing to do with humanitarian aid as such because this aid, particularly in conflict situations, has only one task and responsibility: to preserve life as far as possible.
We are talking about the lives of people who are directly affected by violence; people who are injured, displaced, persecuted or tortured; people who have no water or food, no roof over their heads, no medical assistance.
The Federal Foreign Office has repeatedly described humanitarian aid as one of the priorities of German foreign policy
Independently of political aims, humanitarian organisations are responsible for finding the people most in need and supporting them until they are able to look after themselves again or until the necessary structures and institutions have been restored.
This shows the complex balancing act between foreign and security policy on the one hand and humanitarian aid on the other.
This becomes difficult in cases where the German Government has major political and military interests.
In such situations, there is often an overwhelming temptation to make use of everyone, including humanitarian organisations, for political objectives.
And doing so seems to make sense to many people.
It is no wonder that humanitarian workers are turned back in many parts of the world and even targeted by violence in extreme cases.
One of the consequences of this is that far too many people in life-threatening situations do not receive the help they need because it is too dangerous for the aid organisations to even meet them in order to find out about they problems they are facing.
Médecins Sans Frontières @ msf_de – “Humanitarian aid must not be an instrument of foreign policy” #review2014
and says that the humanitarian aid financed by the German Government satisfies the internationally recognised humanitarian principles, particularly impartiality, independence and neutrality.
The result is that the population and armed actors, particularly in conflict zones, often question the neutrality and independence of humanitarian aid in general.
Many different actors are involved.
First of all, there are helpers on the ground – mainly the neighbours, friends and families of the people in need; then there are aid organisations – local and sometimes international organisations, at times a large number of the latter (such as after the earthquake in Haiti in 2010) or just a few organisations (such as in the Central African Republic at the beginning of 2014); and finally there are the UN organisations, the International Red Cross, NGOs and many governments, including the German Government, which is represented by the Federal Foreign Office in this case.

From the very beginning, the Federal Government has attached special priority to the process of providing moral and financial compensation for the crimes committed by the National Socialist regime.
There were legal reasons for this, quite apart from the financial consequences of a broader compensation package – the compensation provided for war damages should, as normal under international law, remain without prejudice to any state-to-state reparation payments, and should therefore not be provided in the form of payments to individual foreigners.
An exception was made for Israel, since the state was not founded until 1948 and was therefore not a wartime enemy of Germany.
Persecuted Jews who were imprisoned in a concentration camp or ghetto for three months or who lived either in hiding or illegally using a false identity for six months can be granted a monthly pension for the rest of their lives.

The states of the Eastern Partnership: Ukraine, Moldova, Georgia, Belarus, Armenia and Azerbaijan (in orange) © Kolja21 via Wikimedia Commons
The Eastern Partnership was launched in 2009 (Prague, 7 May 2009) by Germany and its European partners along with the EU’s neighbours Ukraine, Moldova, Georgia, Belarus, Armenia and Azerbaijan.
The decision to establish the Eastern Partnership had been taken by the EU Heads of State and Government at their summit on 19 and 20 March 2009 with a view to promoting political association and economic integration with these eastern neighbours.
Family photo at the 2009 Prague Summit © picture alliance/dpa
Following the historic changes in the former Soviet Union, and given our shared values, the Partnership provides an opportunity to support our eastern partners on their way to becoming democratic societies based on the rule of law.
That is why visa liberalisation is one of the Eastern Partnership’s long-term goals.
It is based in the first instance on the conclusion of comprehensive association agreements with the EU, a fundamental part of which comprises DCFTAs (Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Agreements).
Germany is committed to the Eastern Partnership: Federal Chancellor Merkel at the summit in Warsaw in 2011 © picture alliance/dpa
At the same time, the Eastern Partnership aims to promote enhanced cooperation between all the partners.
Corresponding platforms have been set up, which allow projects in these areas to be discussed and agreed upon and in which all EU and partner countries may participate, often in cooperation with international organisations (such as the OSCE or the Council of Europe) or non-governmental organisations.
Projects currently under way cover a broad spectrum, ranging from disaster prevention to support for small and medium-sized enterprises to internet-based school partnerships.
since Crimea was annexed in violation of international law and eastern Ukraine has been destabilised, the country has been in a state of serious crisis.
Ukrainian President Poroshenko and Federal Chancellor Merkel at the signing of the association agreements with Moldova, Georgia and Ukraine in Brussels on 27 June 2014 © dpa/picture alliance
This occasion prompted EU Council President Herman Van Rompuy to speak of “a great day for Europe”, one which, according to him, future generations in Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia would remember.
This also involves the deployment of an Association Council, which will closely guide and evaluate the association process and will be supported by an association committee and subcommittees.
After Russia exerted its influence and Armenia announced that it would join the Eurasian Customs Union, the association and free trade agreement which had been negotiated could no longer be signed, as membership of the Customs Union is not compatible with an EU free trade agreement.
The negotiations with Azerbaijan are not yet ready for conclusion, but there has been some progress.
Given the political situation in Belarus, there can be no negotiations on any further intensification of bilateral relations at present.
The 2013 Eastern Partnership summit in Vilnius
The following points were achieved at the summit in Vilnius (28 to 29 November 2013):
Adoption of a Joint Declaration of the Eastern Partnership Summit
Initialling of association agreements with Georgia and Moldova
Signing of a framework agreement with Georgia on participation in EU crisis management operations
Signing of a visa facilitation agreement with Azerbaijan
Adoption of a joint statement with Armenia
The implementation of the comprehensive association agendas and free trade agreements now stands at the fore.
A successful implementation process is the prerequisite for achieving the goal of unprecedented political and economic integration set by Germany and its partners in the Eastern Partnership.
Logo of the Eastern Partnership © EU
These summits are the forum for the political steering of the process.
Following the founding summit in Prague in 2009, the second summit, held in Warsaw on 29 and 30 September 2011, primarily concentrated on how to take the Eastern Partnership forward.
Lithuania hosted the third Eastern Partnership Summit in Vilnius on 28 and 29 November 2013.
The 2015 Summit will take place in Riga.
Germany is also active in other formats among particularly committed EU member states in seeking the further development of the Eastern Partnership.
In November 2010, Berlin hosted the Second Eastern Partnership Civil Society Forum, which brought together over 200 representatives of civil society organisations from across the EU and from partner countries.
A further forum took place in Poznań (Poland) in 2011, and another was held in Stockholm in November 2012.
On 4 and 5 October 2013 the Republic of Moldova hosted the Civil Society Forum on Working Together for a European Future, becoming the first of the partner countries to do so.
In 2014, the annual meeting of the Civil Society Forum took place in Tbilisi, Georgia, on 20 and 21 November.
Under the keynote heading “EU Integration and Common Security: Making it Happen”, more than 250 representatives of civil society organisations in all six Eastern Partnership countries and the EU discussed topics including free elections, the media and freedom of expression, corruption, visa liberalisation, energy and human rights and formulated policy recommendations.
In addition, joint principles were laid down for the civil society platforms to be included in the association agreements with Ukraine, Georgia and the Republic of Moldova.
Until the agreements enter fully into force following their complete ratification by the EU, the partner countries and all EU Member States, parts of the agreements (provided they are not the responsibility of the Member States) will be provisionally applied by the EU and the partner country in question.
Germany has already started the ratification process for all three agreements.

The European External Action Service (EEAS)

The EEAS is an institution independent of the Council and the Commission.
The units (with over 1500 staff) previously dealing with external relations in the Council Secretariat and the Commission have been integrated into the new organisation.
The EEAS has its headquarters in Brussels and around 140 EU Delegations (“EU embassies”) in third countries and at international organisations.
In late July 2010, the Council approved the arrangements for the organisation and functioning of the EEAS.
The organisation and functioning of the European External Action Service shall be established by a decision of the Council.
The EU’s crisis management structures have also been integrated into the EEAS.

Website of the European External Action Service
One of the major reforms introduced by the Treaty of Lisbon, which entered into force on 1 December 2009, was the creation of a European External Action Service (EEAS)
One of the main objectives of the Treaty of Lisbon is to make the EU more effective and coherent in the field of external action.
The Treaty of Lisbon created the post of High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy.
The Council appointed former Italian foreign minister Federica Mogherini as the new High Representative as of 1 November 2014.
From November 2009 to October 2014, the position was held by Baroness Catherine Ashton of the UK.
The High Representative serves as one of the Vice-Presidents of the European Commission, and is also charged with coordinating other aspects of external action on its behalf.
The new role of High Representative brings together three functions that had previously been performed by different people: the former High Representative for the Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP), the former Commissioner for External Relations and the former chair of the Foreign Affairs Council (a post that previously rotated between the Member States).
She represents the EU on CFSP issues, a role previously fulfilled by the rotating Presidency.
The relevant provision of the Treaty on European Union (Article 27 (3)) is as follows:
It works closely with the diplomatic services of the Member States.
The European External Action Service (EEAS) supports the High Representative in performing the tasks laid down for this role in the Treaty of Lisbon, both in the CFSP/CSDP sphere and as Vice-President of the European Commission.
“[The European External Action Service] shall work in cooperation with the diplomatic services of the Member States and shall comprise officials from relevant departments of the General Secretariat of the Council and of the Commission as well as staff seconded from national diplomatic services of the Member States.
The Corporate Board assisting the High Representative comprises an Executive Secretary General, two Deputy Secretaries General and a Chief Operating Officer.
Below them there are seven Managing Directors in charge of regional units (Asia; Europe/Russia/Central Asia; Middle East; North/Central/South America; Africa), issues-based units (e.g. multilateral affairs, human rights, crisis response and security) and human resources and finances.
They plan and organise EU missions within the scope of the Common Security and Defence Policy (CSDP).
and are seconded to the EEAS for a limited period.
Stephan Auer was appointed Director of Multilateral Relations and Global Issues, while Roland Schäfer serves as Director for the Americas at the EEAS headquarters.
German diplomats also hold important posts in the EU Delegations – e.g. in Geneva, Luanda and Washington – as well as at the EEAS headquarters in Brussels.
The Treaty of Lisbon, which entered into force on 1 December 2009, created the European External Action Service (EEAS).
Federica Mogherini, the High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, with German Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier
The EEAS began its work in December 2010.
Following a phase of extensive development, it has raised the EU’s visibility in the field of foreign policy.
The EEAS has a large number of employees from the EU Member States, including Germany.

Thirty-five very long seconds: Recalling the earthquake of 12 January 2010 in Haiti
On 12 January 2010, Haiti was struck by a magnitude 7.0 earthquake, killing approximately 250,000 people and making some 1.5 million homeless.
The then German Ambassador in Port-au-Prince, Jens-Peter Voss, recalls the earthquake and its immediate aftermath.
On Tuesday afternoon at 5 p.m. – seven minutes before the end of the working day – the earthquake strikes.
The Head of the German Embassy in Port-au-Prince, Jens-Peter Voss, his staff and his wife are in the premises of the chancery when a magnitude 7.0 earthquake lasting 35 seconds rocks Haiti.
“Thirty-five seconds that can be very long”, Voss recalls today.
The people cried for help, he said – “otherwise we stood under the door frame, which is what you are told to do in the event of an earthquake”.

Germany’s financial contribution to the United Nations
UN regular budget
Peacekeeping
For the peacekeeping missions, Germany is the fourth largest contributor in 2014 after France (7.2 percent), because the Permanent Members of the Security Council pay a larger contribution on account of their special responsibility.
The United States is the largest contributor with 28.4 percent.
Japan is in second place with 10.8 percent.
Additional obligatory and voluntary contributions
The two-year budget amounts to almost 5.8 billion US dollars, of which Germany contributes 7.1 percent (approximately 190 million US dollars each year).
This makes Germany the third-largest contributor to the regular budget, behind the United States (22 percent) and Japan (10.8 percent).
Other important contributors are our EU partners the United Kingdom (5.2 percent), France (5.6 percent) and Italy (4.4 percent).
The budgets for the individual peacekeeping operations are each passed separately for one year, running from July to the following June.

UN Security Council Resolution 1325
Thanks to its focus, the project will help implement UN Security Council Resolution 1325 on “Women, Peace and Security”.

Assuming a share in the responsibility for world affairs
International United Nations peace missions with German involvement
Support for the UN’s Standby Arrangements System (UNSAS)
Germany plays a major and active role both in conflict prevention efforts and in international peace missions, contributing peacekeepers, police officers, civilian experts, funding and equipment.
Since the beginning of 2013 Germany’s contribution has amounted to 7.1%.
“We have come to assume a share in the responsibility for world affairs on the basis of our convictions and within the scope of our possibilities.”

Our biggest UN contingent are the around 150 soldiers serving with UNIFIL in Lebanon.
Germany also has soldiers and/or police officers serving with the UN-led missions MINURSO (Western Sahara), MINUSMA (Mali), UNMISS (South Sudan), UNAMID (Sudan), UNMIL (Liberia), UNMIK (Kosovo) and UNAMA (Afghanistan).
German nationals are further deployed on the following international missions:

The UN’s Standby Arrangements System (UNSAS) was set up in 1994 to reduce the time required for a UN peace mission to become operational once mandated by the UN Security Council.
Under this system UN member countries designate military and civilian assets and capabilities that, on request and following governmental approval in any given case, the UN may in principle draw on for peacekeeping purposes.
UNSAS provides for four different levels of participation.
Level One means participating countries designate specific civilian and military capabilities.
Level Two means countries provide detailed planning data.
With Level Three countries enter into a contractual agreement to provide specific forces.
Germany joined UNSAS on 24 July 1998,
offering in principle to provide exclusively civilian contributions (medical and technical support) for UN peace missions.
In a further agreement concluded on 1 November 2000 Germany offered to provide also military contributions, notably
land and aerial transport, medical and engineering components, telecommunications and related security units, naval reconnaissance, monitoring and mine defence components, military observers, military police units and command support personnel.
Since the latter’s accession to the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990, the reunited Germany has been a member of the organisation as one state.

The new Human Rights Council convened for the first time from 19 to 30 June 2006.
What is new about the Human Rights Council?
The Council meets for ten weeks per year spread over three sessions.
The Human Rights Council now has an Advisory Committee consisting of 18 experts.
With the Universal Periodic Review, the Human Rights Council has established a procedure under which all UN member states have to submit to a periodic review mechanism to ensure that they are meeting their human rights obligations.
Under this new procedure, the Human Rights Council examines the human rights situation in each UN member state at four-yearly intervals.
The country in question presents its report and, in the course of an interactive dialogue before the Human Rights Council lasting three and a half hours, responds to the questions and recommendations of other states.
The human rights situation in Germany was first reviewed by the Human Rights Council on 2 February 2009.
Germany was reviewed for a second time on 25 April 2013.

The Helsinki Final Act (1975), the Charter of Paris (1990), the Charter for European Security adopted in Istanbul in 1999 and the Astana Declaration “Towards a Security Community” (2010) are the OSCE’s key documents, defining a steadily evolving and maturing set of political commitments based on a broad understanding of security.
This understanding of security includes the so-called “three dimensions” of the OSCE:
The most important goals of the OSCE thus include establishing comprehensive and indivisible security, conflict prevention and conflict management in all phases of conflicts and crisis in the OSCE region, protection of human rights, democratic and rule-of-law standards as a contribution to security and stability, disarmament, confidence building measures and fighting terrorism.
All 57 OSCE participating States enjoy equal status.
Decisions are taken by consensus and are politically, but not legally binding.
The Chairman-in-Office (Serbia in 2015) bears overall responsibility for executive action.
It is supported by the previous and succeeding chairs (Switzerland in 2014, Germany in 2016), who together with the Chairman-in-Office form the so-called Troika.
OSCE Secretary General Zannier (file photo)
The Secretary General (since July 2011 Ambassador Lamberto Zannier from Italy) supports the Chairperson-in-Office and heads the OSCE Secretariat,
which has a staff of about 310.
the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) in Warsaw (www.osce.org/odihr),
the High Commissioner on National Minorities (HCNM), based in The Hague (www.osce.org/hcnm),
and the OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media in Vienna (www.osce.org/fom).
The public’s attention is currently focused on the OSCE’s engagement in Ukraine.
In addition to this, as Special Representative of the OSCE Chairperson-in-Office, Swiss diplomat Heidi Tagliavini participates in the Trilateral Contact Group (comprised of a representative from Ukraine, Russia and the OSCE respectively).
This group provides the framework for the details of implementing the Minsk agreements of 5 September 2014 to be negotiated.
The CSCE’s traditional role as a forum for political consultation and negotiation has, due to many internal and inter-ethnic conflicts, gradually expanded in the recent years to include new functions in the areas of early warning, conflict prevention and post-conflict peacebuilding.
The OSCE Ministerial Council unanimously voted for this on 5 December.
Germany has been a member of the so-called OSCE Troika since 1 January 2015.
Germany is an active contributor of finance and personnel to the OSCE,
German staff are to be found in almost all the OSCE long-term missions and in OSCE institutions.
All in all, Germany seconds 55 experts.
Furthermore, Germany regularly contributes up to 15 percent – which is actually the limit prescribed by the OSCE – to the election observation missions run by the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR).
In order to strengthen the participation of academic institutions in security policy discussions, together with France, Poland and Russia, Germany announced the establishment of IDEAS: Initiative for the Development of a Euro-Atlantic and Eurasian Security Community.

Greece:
Negotiations in Dayton
The arms control section of the Dayton Peace Agreement concluded on 21 November 1995 by the parties to the conflict in the former Yugoslavia has proven to be an effective regional confidence-building and arms-control instrument and has led to a considerable reduction in the parties’ arms stockpiles and troop strengths, which today lie well below the agreed ceilings.
The parties to the Agreement today are Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro and Serbia.
In Annex 1B (Agreement on Regional Stabilisation), the Dayton Agreement contains two sections on arms-control issues that are still relevant.
Article IV:
Negotiations on numerical limits on holdings of heavy arms systems and on voluntary troop ceilings.
Article V:
Negotiations between all parties and (unnamed) neighbouring states on a regional arms control agreement to establish a “regional balance in and around the former Yugoslavia” under the auspices of the OSCE Forum on Security Co-operation (FSC).
Article IV
The implementation of Article IV was laid down in the Florence Agreement of 14 June 1996.
It sets out ceilings for five categories of armaments (battle tanks, armoured combat vehicles, artillery, combat aircraft and attack helicopters) for the former parties to the conflict.
The parties’ troop levels have been limited by unilaterally declared voluntary ceilings.
The Agreement also contains provisions on a comprehensive annual exchange of information on armaments and personnel levels.
Moreover, it provides for a strict verification regime with the participation of the Personal Representative of the OSCE Chairman-in-Office for Article IV of the Dayton Peace Agreement and the support of third states.
The core arms control requirements have now been fulfilled, since the limits on armaments and manpower have been met and the prescribed reductions in stockpiles completed.
The OSCE participating states agreed to appoint a Personal Representative of the Chairman-in-Office for Article IV at the 1995 OSCE Ministerial Council in Budapest.
The position was held by the Italian Major-General Michele Torres from September 2011 to the end of 2014,
when the office of the Personal Representative in Vienna was officially closed.
At the OSCE Ministerial Council in Basel in December 2014, the transfer of ownership was signed by the states parties in the presence of representatives of the countries of the Contact Group (the US, Russian Federation, France, Great Britain, Italy and Germany).
With that the four states parties, Serbia, Croatia, Montenegro and Bosnia and Herzegovina assumed ownership for the tasks relating to implementing the Agreement.
The OSCE Conflict Prevention Centre provides them with logistical support for this.
Up to the end of 2014, Germany provided personnel and equipment to help implement the Agreement, for example by seconding personnel to the Personal Representative of the OSCE Chairman-in-Office and providing support for inspections.
The implementation of Article IV is still monitored by a Sub-Regional Consultative Commission, which is composed of representatives of the parties and meets regularly.
Representatives of the Contact Group will continue to take part in these sessions, as they have done to date.
Article V
Article V of Annex 1B to the Dayton Agreement was superseded by the adoption of a politically binding Final Document, which has been in force since 1 January 2002.
Participating states are Albania, Austria, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Macedonia, Montenegro (since January 2007), the Netherlands, Romania, Russia, Serbia, Slovenia, Spain, the United Kingdom, the USA, and Turkey.
The original goal of negotiating a nuanced regional arms control agreement had to be abandoned due to the resistance of some of the states.
Nevertheless, the Final Document does provide a framework for intensified regional and border-region confidence- and security-building measures between all states in the Balkans and neighbouring countries, albeit on a voluntary basis.
A commission comprising representatives from the participating states monitors the implementation of the voluntary measures and informs the OSCE Forum on Security Co-operation (FSC) and Permanent Council of activities.
Germany supports the implementation of the Final Document by states in the region, for example through bilateral measures such as support for training, fact-finding visits, language courses as well as by participating in mutual inspection visits and actively promoting the Centre for Security Cooperation (RACVIAC, Regional Arms Control Verification and Implementation Assistance Center) in Zagreb.
RACVIAC – Centre for Security Cooperation
The Regional Centre for Security Cooperation (which is known as RACVIAC, formerly called the Regional Arms Control Verification and Implementation Assistance Centre) in Zagreb was founded in 2000 at Germany’s initiative as a German-Croatian project under the Stability Pact for South Eastern Europe.
Its initial focus was on strengthening cooperative security and confidence-building in South Eastern Europe, and in particular providing training for verification staff to implement the Dayton Peace Agreement.
However, it soon evolved into a regional forum for dialogue on all issues of regional security, offering seminars and further training in three areas: cooperative security, security sector reform and international cooperation.
It has thus become an established player, making an important contribution to confidence-building in the region.
RACVIAC was given a new legal basis in 2011 with the ratification of the new Agreement.
This is a multilateral instrument between Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, Montenegro, Romania, Serbia and Turkey.
RACVIAC thus became a regionally owned organisation.
Germany is an associate member.
The German Government continues to provide financial support for the Centre’s work (45,000 euros in 2014) and to send instructors for the various seminars.

“Since wars begin in the minds of men, it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed.”
This is UNESCO’s guiding principle.
From the experience of the Second World War, it learned the lesson that “a peace based exclusively upon the political and economic arrangements of governments would not be a peace which could secure the unanimous, lasting and sincere support of the peoples of the world,
and the peace must therefore be founded, if it is not to fail, upon the intellectual and moral solidarity of mankind” (from the Constitution of UNESCO, signed on 16 November 1945).
The current Director-General is Irina Bokova of Bulgaria, who took office in November 2009.
UNESCO’s main decision-making body is the General Conference of its 193 member states.
In 2013, Germany was elected to the Executive Board for a four-year term.
The Executive Board, UNESCO’s political steering body, monitors implementation of the programme adopted by the General Conference.
UNESCO is financed by regular obligatory contributions from its member states as well as extrabudgetary voluntary funding.
The latter accounted for around 47% of all the funds UNESCO had at its disposal in 2013.
The regular two-year budget for 2014/2015 amounted to 653 million US dollars.
At the governmental level, summits take place every two years, alternating with biennial meetings of foreign ministers.

The United Nations Children’s Fund estimates that globally some 130 million women and girls suffer female genital mutilation, every year some three million young girls are subject to the practice.
Female genital mutilation involves partial or total removal of the external female genitalia.
In particularly severe cases the vagina is sewn shut, leaving only a small opening.
Female genital mutilation is practised in 28 countries in Africa but also in the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula and in some countries in Asia.
Migration has since brought FGM to North America and Europe, too, including Germany.
Female genital mutilation is a serious violation of human rights and an expression of discrimination and violence against women.
The German Government is therefore working actively both in Germany and beyond to bring about the elimination of this practice.

Economic relations
Lemon harvest in South Africa
Africa has tremendous economic potential which is increasingly being developed.
Around a billion people live on the continent, and at over 1000 US dollars, Africa’s per-capita GNP is higher than that of some G20 countries.
The World Bank says this (middle income) level should be reached in almost all countries on the continent by 2025.
Over the last ten years, the continent’s GDP has risen by 30 percent.
Growth rates remain at 5 percent on average.
More and more sub-Saharan African states can be found in the top 100 countries in the World Bank’s annual Doing Business Report, including Botswana, Ghana, Mauritius, Namibia, Rwanda and Zambia.
African states are becoming more and more integrated into global trade.
Africa’s trade in goods and especially raw materials with the Asia-Pacific region (particularly China), Europe and North America, but also India, is seeing above-average growth.
This is increasing demand for the expansion and improvement of infrastructure – railways, roads, ports and logistics, pipelines and air traffic.
Major producer of commodities and energy
In recent years Africa has become a much more important trade and investment partner for Germany, not only because it is an emerging producer of commodities and energy, but also in the manufacturing sector and tourism.
In 2013, however, German-African external trade fell to 26 billion euros (down 2.8 percent on the previous year).
German exports totalled 13.6 billion euros, also slightly down on the previous year.
Imports totalled 12.4 billion euros.
Energy imports and agricultural products still account for the lion’s share of imports from Africa.
As in previous years, Germany’s main exports to Africa were vehicles, machinery and chemical products.
There are still obstacles to development
Growing flowers in Kenya
In 2013 South Africa was again Germany’s major trading partner in sub-Saharan Africa, with a volume of trade totalling 13.2 billion euros.
In 2009 the volume of trade was just 9.7 billion euros.
Second place in 2013 was again taken by Nigeria.
But this trend cannot hide the fact that Africa still plays a relatively minor role for German business compared to other parts of the world, accounting for no more than about 1.3 percent of German foreign trade.
In many countries lack of infrastructure, corruption, political instability and non-transparency still block economic development.
African regional organisations such as SADC, ECOWAS and EAC are increasingly trying to make the region more attractive for foreign investment and cooperation by taking steps towards regional economic integration (e.g. common markets, customs and currency unions).
The German Government is working to enable German companies, especially SMEs, to have a fair chance in global competition in Africa; to this end, it has created a wide range of instruments to promote and finance foreign trade and investment.

Contributions to peacekeeping
UNESCO (United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization), which was founded in 1945, is the United Nations’ agency for education, science, culture and communication.
Its aim is to maintain peace and contribute towards security by fostering international cooperation in education, science, culture and communication.
The Federal Republic of Germany became a member of UNESCO on 11 July 1951, while the GDR joined in 1972.
It convenes in Paris every two years and sets the organisation’s general priorities as well as its programme and budget.
It is also responsible for electing the Executive Board, which is made up of 58 representatives of the member states and meets twice a year.
Germany’s Permanent Delegation to UNESCO in Paris
Germany’s Permanent Delegation to UNESCO in Paris maintains ongoing working contacts with the UNESCO Secretariat and is responsible for cultivating relations with UNESCO.

Film co‑production agreement signed with the Netherlands
Promoting German‑Dutch film co-production
On 7 February, Germany and the Netherlands signed an intergovernmental agreement on the co-production of films at the 65th Berlinale.
On Saturday (7 February), Germany and the Netherlands signed an intergovernmental agreement on the co-production of films at the 65th Berlinale in Berlin.
The Dutch Minister of Education, Culture and Science, Jet Bussemaker, travelled to the German capital to sign the agreement, which aims to facilitate joint film productions in the future.
On the German side, the agreement was signed by the Federal Government Commissioner for Culture and the Media, Monika Grütters, and the Director-General for Culture and Communication at the Federal Foreign Office, Andreas Görgen.
Among the guests were the directors of the German Federal Film Board (FFA) and the Netherlands Film Fund (NFF) – Peter Dinges and Doreen Boonekamp – who also welcomed the signing of the agreement.
Greater support for co-productions
The German-Dutch film agreement constitutes the legal framework for cooperation between German and Dutch film producers.
Furthermore, it contains regulations that go beyond the European Convention on Cinematographic Co-production.
Under its terms, films co-produced by German and Dutch film makers will be treated and supported as national productions.
The agreement therefore allows co-producers to access national public funds in both countries.
Once the new regulations have entered into force, German-Dutch co-producers will be able to cooperate more flexibly and effectively, ultimately to the benefit of cinema visitors.
Two German-Dutch co-productions are being screened at the 65th Berlinale, with Nena by Saskia Diesing and Zurich by Sacha Polak.

Ensuring that Germany has a sustainable, secure and cost-effective supply of energy and raw materials is another important aim of our cooperation with the region.
The German Government is accordingly supporting efforts by countries in the region to develop sustainable energy systems by providing advice, funding projects and concluding energy and climate protection agreements.
The challenge is to access new markets, particularly in the field of renewable energies, energy efficiency and environmental technology, as well as in the production of raw materials.
As a country with few raw materials, Germany is dependent on imports to supply its needs.
This goes not only for energy but also for metals.
The German Government’s raw materials policy therefore attaches great importance to security of supply, alongside economic efficiency and environmentally responsible production.
Latin America has rich deposits of minerals such as iron, copper, tin and lithium.
Just under 60% of the global production of lithium – important, for instance, for the production of lithium-ion batteries for electric cars – comes from Latin America.
As this example makes clear, cooperation with Latin America is, for Germany in particular with its advanced technology industries, crucial for the development and introduction of technologies that in the future will play a major role.

The German rules on citizenship were thoroughly revised with the entry into force of the amended Nationality Act (Staatsangehörigkeitsgesetz) on 1 January 2000.
The Act was further revised with the entry into force of the main part of the Immigration Act (Zuwanderungsgesetz) on 1 January 2005 and its further provisions on 28 August 2007.
On 20 December 2014 the Second Act Amending the Nationality Act entered into force.
This contains new provisions concerning the obligation for children born in Germany to non-German parents to choose one nationality (Optionsregelung).
Provisions for non-Germans living in Germany
Since 2000, children born in Germany to non-German parents automatically acquire German citizenship if one parent has been legally resident in Germany for at least eight years and has a permanent right of residence.
However, the Second Act Amending the Nationality Act, which entered into force on 20 December 2014, significantly reduces the number of those obliged to opt for one nationality.
As a general rule, non-Germans have the right to become naturalised after eight years of legal residence in Germany, provided they meet the relevant conditions.
However, since 1 January 2000 the exceptions that allow applicants to retain their former nationality have been considerably broader.
Since 28 August 2007, nationals of EU member states and Switzerland who are naturalised in Germany have been allowed to hold multiple nationality.
If you are a non-German living in Germany and have questions about acquiring German nationality, please contact the local authority in the town or district in which you reside.
The nationality law reform does not only affect non-Germans living in Germany, but also Germans living abroad.
Children born abroad to one or more German parents who themselves were born abroad on or after 1 January 2000 (entry into force of the amended Nationality Act), will no longer automatically acquire German nationality.
People who have lost their German nationality by choosing to acquire a foreign nationality (section 25 of the Nationality Act) can now re-acquire their German nationality more easily provided they fulfil certain conditions; the opinion of the responsible German mission abroad carries considerable weight in such cases (section 13 of the Nationality Act).
Non-Germans can also be naturalised while living abroad, provided they have special ties with Germany to justify this (section 14 of the Nationality Act).
However, since 1 January 2000 it has been easier for Germans who acquire a foreign nationality to retain their German nationality.
Since 28 August 2007, Germans acquiring the nationality of another EU member state or Switzerland no longer automatically lose their German nationality,
However, since 6 July 2011, this rule no longer applies to persons who voluntarily serve in the armed forces of an EU member state, a NATO member state, an EFTA country or Australia, New Zealand, Israel or the Republic of Korea.

The top-level talks between Germany, France, Ukraine and Russia on de-escalating the conflict in eastern Ukraine had been ongoing since they started on Wednesday afternoon.
The parties to the conflict finally agreed on a ceasefire which is set to enter into force at 12 a.m. on 15 February as well as a roadmap for the implementation of the Minsk agreements of September 2014.

The Kyoto Protocol – currently the most important global environmental agreement
The Kyoto Protocol was adopted in December 1997 at the 3rd session of the Conference of the Parties (COP 3) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).
It is the most important global environmental agreement.
Over and above its significance as a milestone in global efforts to combat climate change, it has a great impact on development policy and constitutes a new component in the world economic order.
As an element of effective global governance, the Kyoto Protocol is symbolic and acts as a model.
The Kyoto Protocol entered into force on 16 February 2005 following its ratification by Russia in late October 2004,
which meant the condition for entry into force had been met: at least 55 Parties to the UNFCCC, accounting for at least 55% of total CO2 emissions for 1990 of the so-called Annex I Parties (industrialised countries), had ratified it.
The EU member states deposited their instruments of ratification on 31 May 2002.
Among the industrialised countries, only the United States and Australia have not ratified the Protocol.
Australia intends voluntarily to cut its emissions to the level that would have been required if it had ratified the Kyoto Protocol.
The vast majority of emerging economies and developing countries, including China, India and Brazil, have ratified the Protocol.
We are appalled by the news reaching us from Copenhagen.
With the Kyoto Protocol, the international community agreed for the first time on binding targets and measures for combating climate change.
The Kyoto Protocol stipulates global ceilings for greenhouse gas emissions.
The industrialised countries recognise their historical responsibility for global warming: accordingly, they (rather than the developing countries) are taking the first step by undertaking to cut emissions in the first commitment period 2008-2012.
The industrialised countries have recognised their historical responsibility for global warming: accordingly, they (and initially not the developing countries) took the first step by undertaking to cut emissions in the first commitment period 2008-2012.
Besides cutting their own emissions, countries have at their disposal three flexible instruments to help attain this goal: Emissions Trading (global trading in emissions rights), Joint Implementation (technology development and transfer) and the Clean Development Mechanism (implementation of measures in developing countries).
Germany’s commitment
It has lived up to its commitment:
Germany did indeed manage to reduce its emissions by an average of 23.6% in this period.
The Kyoto Protocol’s first commitment period expired at the end of 2012.
At the Conference of the Parties in Durban in 2011 and Qatar in 2012 a second commitment period, to expire in 2020, was agreed.
Further European countries and Australia are participating alongside the (then) 27 EU member states.
They have pledged to reduce their emissions by an average of 18% (as against 1990 levels) over the period 2013-2020.

The UNFCCC – ratified by 196 countries in the world and headquartered in Bonn – is the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change.
It identifies climate change as a serious global problem and commits the international community to combat it.
The Parties to the Convention aim to stabilise greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere at a level that would prevent dangerous human-induced interference with the climate system (global warming).
In order to achieve this goal, the Convention defines the principle of “common but differentiated responsibilities” of industrialised and developing countries in order to take account of their different capabilities and current (as well as historical) emission volumes.
Based on reports compiled by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), it decides on the measures which the parties to the Convention will take to reach their climate targets.
The Kyoto Protocol adopted in December 1997 at the 3rd COP is the most important piece of legislation at global level enacted to date for the protection of the global ecosystem.
In Cancún in December 2010 (COP 16) the states parties managed to agree on provisions for a future climate regime, in particular on funding, deforestation and technological cooperation, as well as the 2˚C limit for global warming.
At the COP 17 which took place in Durban in late 2011, the countries pledged to negotiate a new global climate change agreement by 2015.

When Federal President Joachim Gauck, Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier and Minister of Defence von der Leyen outlined their respective security policy views at the Munich Security Conference in February 2014 the German public reacted with surprise.
The three speeches were interpreted as a renunciation of the culture of military restraint.
It was by no means about a paradigm shift but about further developing our foreign policy.
Yet the debates had also led many people to nurse the fear that stronger foreign policy engagement would inevitably lead to a militarisation of Germany’s foreign policy.
However, the figures tell a different story:
Anyone who measures the quality of Germany’s foreign policy exclusively by the willingness to take military action is ignoring the fact that Germany works with the entire range of its foreign policy tools – from diplomatic mediation to civilian conflict prevention, humanitarian assistance and development cooperation.
When crises and conflicts do not even flare up or escalate then the preventative measures have had the desired effect.
2014 was a difficult year for crisis prevention.
We were forced to be reactive in many trouble spots.
Yet even in acute conflicts we remain committed to prioritising civilian engagement.
Indeed in the Ukraine crisis the German Government made it clear from the outset that
there can be no military solution.
Seldom has the Federal Government wrangled so hard to find a diplomatic solution to a conflict.
The politicians involved showed courage,
and troops ensured success.
And the KFOR stabilisation mission in Kosovo was already a success the day it’s heavily armed international troops marched through the country, making it clear to all that the killing had to stop.
This form of conflict prevention must, therefore, be visible in order to have an effect,
but we Germans tend to have a knee-jerk reaction of trepidation to this.
Yet the equation – the fewer troops we deploy, the more peaceful our foreign policy is – does not add up.
Of course,
There are currently four German soldiers posted in Western Sahara, eight in Somalia, ten in Darfur and 16 in South Sudan.
These smaller engagements are important, too,
Our society’s consensus on the primacy of civilian engagement is particularly strong.
This can make it all the more tempting to completely avoid the uncomfortable discussion about the contribution that troops could make to a responsible foreign policy.

Explaining German positions abroad is in the Federal Foreign Office’s blood.
Worldwide deployment presents particular challenges
Tasks which are performed at various levels domestically (Federation, Länder and municipalities) and by countless authorities are all the responsibility of the Foreign Service abroad and in relation to other countries and international organisations.
Foreign Service members therefore have to assume a broad range of functions depending on their assignment at any given time.
Foreign Service members are deployed all around the world.
The regular staff are subject to so-called rotation.
This requires personnel from all career tracks to change jobs every three to five years.
They are transferred abroad from headquarters, or move from one foreign country to another, or return to headquarters from abroad.
It is therefore not uncommon for staff to move house more than a dozen times during the course of their professional life.
The demands placed on members of the Foreign Service are high, for foreign policy spans no less than the entire palette of government activity in the context of external relations.

“What, if anything, is wrong with German foreign policy?

Over 50 experts from Germany and abroad voiced their opinions, helping to conduct a critical assessment of German foreign policy.
52 articles by 57 authors from 26 countries – all around the world, experts in the field of international relations took up Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier’s invitation to contribute their voice to the debate on reviewing German foreign policy.
From political scientists to trade union leaders, journalists to ex-politicians, a former UN Commissioner to historians and the former Secretary-General of the United Nations – everyone answered the Foreign Minister’s question from their own personal viewpoint, providing an extraordinary range of geographical perspectives and content.
In his speech at the opening conference on 20 May 2014, Steinmeier said that it was important to question some of the supposed certainties of foreign policy, for:
“In a world which, 25 years on from the end of the Cold War, from the collapse of a black and white order that had persisted for decades, has not yet found a new order – In a world like that, German foreign policy cannot do anything else except question itself, and question precisely those certainties which seem to be even more built-in than the old paternoster out there in the foyer.”
Much as experts’ views differ, one thing has become clear, namely that expectations of German foreign policy are very high.
For example, some of the authors called on Germany to “reassume the role of model Europeans” in order to “revitalise the European Union” and “as the recognised leader of Europe, to change the course of world history”.

Facebook chat on Review 2014
That is why one of the conclusions of Review 2014 is
It gives me great pleasure to welcome you to the Weltsaal of the Federal Foreign Office for the closing event of Review 2014.
The year-long process that we have completed bore the title “A Fresh Look at German Foreign Policy”.
I can think of no better context for discussing the outcome of this review than the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP), which has been doing precisely that for over 60 years: taking a fresh look at German foreign policy – and in so doing has helped to shape German foreign policy for over six decades.
I would like also to welcome the members of the Young DGAP who are with us this evening and I'm delighted – and sure that many of you here today will share this sentiment – to be able to start this evening by offering you my congratulations:
on behalf of the entire foreign policy community, I would like to wish the German Council on Foreign Relations many happy returns on its 60th birthday – we will be needing you in the coming 60 years too!
At the beginning of my speech, ladies and gentlemen, I would like to share with you an extract from a letter that I received at the end of last year.
She told me that her school building in Donetsk had been hit several times and been damaged in the fighting between the separatists and the Ukrainian military.
But when winter approached, it became increasingly impossible to carry on teaching as almost all of the windows and doors were destroyed.
Together with the schools division here at the Head Office, our consulate-general in Donetsk therefore got hold of the necessary means, funds and workers, and by the end of January 2015, 125 windows and 21 doors at the secondary school no. 19 were repaired.
Many aspects of the turbulent crisis year and the intensive review year that was 2014 are summed up by this story, as are many of the things that we learned about our own work in the past year.
It’s not about moves on the geo-political chessboard – it’s a about the lives and suffering of people, about the future of children.
We need creativity and vigilance in order to use it wisely in all its diversity.
This is precisely why we took stock of our actions with the Review 2014 process!
We have shown the German public that foreign policy is about more than just two extremes: either just talking or shooting; either futile diplomacy or Bundeswehr deployments abroad.
And we at the Federal Foreign Office, too, have reminded ourselves anew what our work is actually about.
Our work is not about dossiers for the Minister or reporting obligations or our daily diplomatic routine, but about using all the tools we can, however small, to help ease people’s fears and worries in this increasingly dangerous world – to make their lives that little bit more peaceful.
Indeed, ladies and gentlemen, sometimes foreign policy is nothing more and nothing less than a question of repairing school windows destroyed by gunfire!
In contrast perhaps to real life, persistence is a virtue in foreign policy.
This is what Ms Prystuba wrote in her last letter at any rate, and I for my part derive a great deal of confidence from letters such as these – and advocate what a journalist recently termed the “tenacity of diplomacy”.
When I look back at the review year of 2014, one feature stands out particularly clearly: the fact that the strategic review was conducted during a time of acute crises.
While German foreign policy makers were taking stock of their work in Review 2014, they were being put to a very tough test by events around the world.
We have assumed more responsibility – not just arbitrarily, but rather in a forward-looking and persevering manner; proactively, but without being over-confident, and always working in a European and international context.
And, above all, without crude black and white views of the world that, while sometimes helpful as they make our public statements easier, make solutions more difficult.
I am well aware of the fact that, as these crises and our Review coincided, the Federal Foreign Office was put under an enormous amount of strain.
Reality sometimes got ahead of the Review – but, overall, it injected important impetus into the debate.
We have given the public debate about the value and means of diplomacy the attention it deserves, also beyond the wave of crises.
I am most grateful to the experts, scientists and practitioners, from Germany and throughout the world – many of whom are here today; the employees of the Federal Foreign Office, who have examined their own work in a critical light and taken part in the public debate; and one person in particular who made an especially great contribution to this process:
We will have an opportunity to talk in a minute on the podium, but I would like now to offer him my most sincere thanks.
As I have already presented the specific results of the Review to the German Bundestag and here at the Federal Foreign Office today, I will refrain tonight from offering you a blow-by-blow account of the list of individual measures.
What I want to do now is to draw political conclusions from these results,
which all have one important thing in common: they're about taking action!
It cannot be enough for a country such as Germany to analyse and make intelligent statements about world events.
What can I do?
What can German foreign policy do?
What can we and our partners do?
During the Ebola epidemic, for example, we saw that while we react swiftly and professionally when it comes to saving Germans, the transition from a consular to a foreign policy crisis took too much time.
Just one week ago, I was in Colombia, where the President asked us Germans – with our own very specific experience of history and coming to terms with history – to support a national reconciliation process that, after decades of a brutal and gruelling conflict between the state and terrorist groupings, aims to re-unite society.
To do this, we also need the many civilian aid workers from Germany working in crisis regions throughout the world – just take the crucial importance of the OSCE observers in Ukraine, for example, whose mission we are currently strengthening and want to extend.
We want to improve their working conditions – from questions of insurance to remuneration and training – and we want to raise the profile of the Center for International Peace Operations here in Berlin as a sending organisation and improve its performance.
Or, is it a logical consequence for forces and tensions to erupt in a world in which structures of order are increasingly losing influence, a world that is growing ever more intertwined, but whose contrasts are colliding with ever more force at the same time?
Yes, the world is unravelling.
We depend on a rule-based international order more than any other state.
I can say this from the perspective of the economy – with our strong focus on exports, we rely on predictable, solid conditions far beyond our own borders – and I can say this from a human rights perspective – because if the United Nations and its institutions of international order lose their legitimacy, then the most important instruments to safeguard human rights are no longer at our disposal.
We are thus creating a place where we can make extensive use of our most important international order principle, namely multilateralism.
But we could also call it the directorate-general for peace order.
For it is important, beyond the language of international law, beyond the tangle of institutions, to recall what the idea of a multilateral, rights-based order actually embodies, which is the hope for peace!
I think we haven’t done too badly in this respect.
Among the 28 member states of the European Union, historical experiences and emotions vis-à-vis Russia vary most greatly.
The final reports that are on display here, and which some of you are already holding in your hands, by no means amount to general terms and conditions for German foreign policy.
We tried to communicate them, such as the question of supplying weapons to the Kurds in northern Iraq, as transparently and openly as possible – with all the risks and side effects that this entails.
It was an exciting process for all concerned.
I am extremely concerned by the news that Iraqi antiquities have been destroyed by the terrorist group ISIS.
Some of mankind’s cultural treasures are being irretrievably lost.
With hammers and drills the group is inflicting deep wounds on the history, traditions and souls of the people in northern Iraq as well as the entire human race.
We must do all we can to ensure that this barbaric “cultural cleansing” is stopped and punished immediately.
By doing so, the terrorist group is destroying the lives and cultural identities of the local people.
These ruthless attacks on mankind’s cultural property once again show the inhumane face of ISIS.

Nominations announced for 2015 GERMAN FOOTBALL AMBASSADOR
In so doing, they not only function as representatives of German football but also promote the image of their homeland as a whole.
The GERMAN FOOTBALL AMBASSADOR initiative has existed since 2013 to honour their commitment with an annual award, recognising the contributions they make to developing the sport and encouraging social progress in their host countries.
And the nominees are ...
The annual shortlist has once again been drawn up: three individuals have been selected to be honoured in early summer 2015 for the development work they do in sport and society.
The three nominees are Michael Nees, technical director of the Israeli football association and coach of the national under-21s team, who focuses his work on engaging with young people and promoting talent and whose dedication helps underpin positive exchange between Germany and Israel; coaching legend Eckhard Krautzun, who has been all over the planet helping to develop football since coaching the Kenyan national team in 1970, most recently in China from 2002 until 2007; and Jürgen Klinsmann, who was on the team that won the World Cup in 1990, is currently the coach of the US national team and, having taken them to victory in the 2013 Gold Cup and the final 16 in the 2014 World Cup, is managing to transform football in the US from a niche pursuit into an increasingly mainstream sport.
Who picks up the GERMAN FOOTBALL AMBASSADOR award in Berlin this early summer will be decided by a jury comprising kicker sports magazine editor Rainer Holzschuh, footballing icon Uwe Seeler, FFO spokesperson Dr Martin Schäfer, actor Peter Lohmeyer and former professional footballers Doris Fitschen and Lutz Pfannenstiel.
Alongside the jury prize, there will once again be a people’s-choice award.
From mid-March, anyone visiting www.fussballbotschafter.de will be able to vote for one of eleven professional footballers who do something admirable for society.

The Federal Foreign Office’s Political Archive is the “memory of German foreign policy”,

Diplomacy’s Viennese Waltz has become a group dance with changing partners
Diplomacy in the 21st century needs new ways of thinking and acting
Be it through hard or soft power, diplomacy is about advocacy.
By Oliver Will.
Two hundred years after the Congress of Vienna, “modern diplomacy’s first party” (Die Welt, 20.12.2014), 70 years after the end of the Second World War and 25 years after German reunification, it is not only the Federal Foreign Office that is undergoing a review process.
All ministries are asking themselves how effective government action can be shaped in the 21st century.
Foreign policy takes place abroad: true.
Foreign policy takes place at home: true.
External relations are shaped by the Federal Foreign Office: true.
External relations are shaped by the Federal Chancellery, ministries, political foundations, bloggers, migrants, companies, the media, social entrepreneurs, academia, cultural organisations, the Länder, cities and so on: true.
In this case too, both statements are simultaneously correct – and this changes diplomacy.
In a polycentric world, the monologue of the supposedly stronger party is no longer in demand.
Instead, people want dialogue with others, and they also want it outside the establishment’s institutional silos.
For diplomacy, this means that a second, increasingly strong centre of gravity, namely public diplomacy, is emerging alongside what has been the core area of classical diplomacy to date.
Public diplomacy can be regarded as an umbrella term that includes elements such as cultural relations and education policy, nation branding and other soft power components (innovation ability, lifestyle, design etc.)
At the moment, the Federal Foreign Office is already (still?) located at the centre of a national diplomatic system, although this is more by tradition than design (Melissen et al.).
The main challenge will be to design and direct a system in the future to steer networks of actors in accordance with the ministry’s interests and goals.
This leads us to some ideas on new ways of thinking and acting, which can be summarised as hypotheses in ten points.
Foreign policy’s scope for action starts at home.
Without public support and acceptance, this scope declines drastically.
Creating awareness – opening up resonance chambers.
The Review 2014 process, with all its elements, is a starting point for this.
The idea is to take a fresh look at foreign policy with all stakeholders.
Defining key messages.
Germany is a diverse country (federalism, economic structure, etc.).
It has an equally high number of foreign policy aims – and an equally low amount of prioritisation in these aims.
A foreign policy “storyline” should be developed along the concepts of diversity, world-mindedness, innovation, ideas, consensus and cooperation.
Although these are abstract concepts, they are very valuable as brand claims and messages that lend a structure to topics and campaigns.
In a fragmented and fragile world, they serve as a bridge and are highly relevant to the future.
Retaining target groups’ loyalty – identifying and reaching new target groups.
There is a need to identify new target groups (migrants, NGOs, social entrepreneurs, internet activists etc.) and to develop communication tools suited to these groups in order to achieve an oscillating balance between the old and new elites in the Federal Foreign Office’s communication strategy.
Foreign policy in networks – organising and steering networks of actors.
The methods of classical diplomacy can only go so far in dealing with the new complexity.
This makes it necessary to establish networks of actors in line with one’s interests, as well as an integrative foreign policy that pursues its aims systematically in a network with actors, including actors outside the institutions with which foreign policymakers have worked to date (Hüttemann, inter alia).
New diplomats for a polycentric, fragmented and fragile world order.
Diplomats’ (self-)image is changing (Thomas Bagger’s concept of network diplomacy, the “interconnected diplomat”).
This has an impact on the skills and qualifications that diplomats have traditionally needed.
There is a need for boundary spanners between actors in various sectors, that is, people with the right language skills and ability to empathise.
Digital diplomacy – an internal and external challenge.

Making global governance more democratic
Better efficiency and credibility through a global parliamentary assembly
The system of global governance is going through a crisis of efficiency and credibility.
At the same time, in light of the current crises and rising number of transnational challenges it is clear that it is more important than ever to have a functioning global order underpinned by corresponding organisations.
Andreas Bummel and Michael Puntschuh call for this in their article.
The system of global governance is increasingly losing credibility.
In important policy fields it is either not providing for durable solutions at all, or not doing so fast enough.
A lack of clarity, instability and chaos are defining features of this world order.
Countless examples could be given,
the United Nations is struggling to fulfil its fundamental task, namely to ensure peace and security.
In West Africa the infectious disease Ebola, which we have known about for decades, is putting stability in the region at risk.
Ever more governments in the world are failing to carry out the basic functions incumbent on a state.
Climate change is in turn threatening the stability of the entire planet;
He added that the foreign ministers agreed that the conflict had “not yet turned a corner”, but rather a positive dynamic now needed to be created.
we do not have an effective international climate regime.
Moreover, in a world of plenty, 1.2 billion people continue to live in extreme poverty and over 800 million in hunger.
However, its inability to provide results is only one side of the credibility crisis afflicting our system of global governance.
The other relates to the architecture of the system itself.
Its lacks transparency, is fragmented and above all undemocratic.
Rectifying these problems could also present a path out of the efficiency crisis.
The more policy fields become globalised, the more the long-bemoaned democratic deficit is worsening.
The times in which international law simply served as rules of the road for states, enabling them to clearly separate domestic and foreign policy, are long gone.
Nevertheless, governments insist on retaining an exclusive mandate over the field of international relations.
In contrast to lobbyists, elected members of parliament have just as little meaningful access to the intergovernmental sphere as civil society.
Institutions such as the United Nations are thus marginalised when it comes to the policy fields in question.
Yet this tendency towards club governance is not surprising –
in the United Nations a country such as Vanuatu carries the same weight as the People’s Republic of China, which has 5600 times the population.
That is no longer sufficient within the framework of international public policy.
The executive only represents the majority opinion,
but representatives of the parliamentary opposition or of minorities also need to have the chance to bring their opinion to the table.
Setting up a global parliamentary assembly has been suggested as a possible means of reducing the democratic deficit of global governance.
Since 2007, a global alliance of hundreds of members of parliament, non-governmental organisations, academics and prominent international figures have worked towards creating such a United Nations Parliamentary Assembly (UNPA).
The assembly would enable, for the first time, not only diplomats appointed by government executives but also members of parliament representing the people to take on a direct and important role in shaping global policy.
This would pave the way for debates in which the primary aim is not to advance national interests but rather to improve overall global well-being.
Moreover, he said, the steps towards implementing the agreement must be monitored and verified, with the OSCE playing a key role in this regard.
The Federal Foreign Office thinks that the parliamentary dimension of international cooperation is already fulfilled by the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU).
However, in reality the IPU does not play any noteworthy role in global governance or within the United Nations.
Moreover, its sole task involves interparliamentary exchange.
The European Parliament proposes equipping the Assembly with “genuine rights of information, participation and control”.
In December 2013, the United Nations Association of Germany (UNA-Germany) called on the new Federal Government and the German Bundestag to draft proposals for the establishment of a UNPA.
A recommendation adopted by the Association advocates that the Assembly enshrine “parliamentary participation and control at the level of the United Nations”.
Over 100 members of the German Bundestag and some 40 German NGOs had already backed the proposal, including Attac, BUND / Friends of the Earth Germany, the Society for Threatened Peoples, Mehr Demokratie e.V., the Senate of the Economy or World Vision in Germany.

Bosnia and Herzegovina’s EU perspective
In December 2014, the EU adopted a renewed approach aimed at drawing Bosnia and Herzegovina closer to the EU, thus ending years of stagnation.
In view of this, on 16 December 2014 the EU adopted a restructured process.
As well as initially focusing on socio-economic reforms, the country’s institutions at all levels of government should be made more effective in the course of the approximation process.
A new timetable was drawn up for existing demands in order to inject new impetus into the approximation process and thus also into the domestic reform process.
Bosnia and Herzegovina’s political leadership, as well as its Parliament, committed themselves irrevocably in writing to reforms in line with the new EU approach on 23 February 2015.
At the same time, the EU and Bosnia and Herzegovina will draft an initial reform agenda which will mainly address socio-economic issues.
Support focuses on boosting agriculture and rural development, improving infrastructure, establishing and protecting independent media, implementing judicial reforms and modernising the country’s economic structures.
